title: How far can you ride a motorcycle in a day?
alt: Motorcyclist riding along a long straight road through a desert landscape toward distant mountains
excerpt: Most riders are comfortable covering 300 to 500 km a day, and experienced tourers manage more. Here is how to work out a realistic daily distance for your bike, your roads and your body.
meta: Most riders manage 300 to 500 km (200 to 300 miles) a day on a motorcycle. Plan a realistic daily distance with a worked example and checklist.

body.p: Most riders can comfortably cover 300 to 500 km (about 200 to 300 miles) in a day on a motorcycle, with experienced touring riders on suitable bikes managing 600 to 800 km on main roads. The real limit is rarely the bike: it is your fatigue, the type of road, the weather and how many stops you need, so a good daily distance is one you can finish still alert enough to ride well.

body.h: Typical daily distances by type of riding

body.p: These are realistic figures for a reasonably fit rider on a bike that suits the job, riding six to eight hours including stops. Treat them as a starting point rather than a target.

ul: Twisty mountain or coastal roads: 200 to 300 km (125 to 185 miles). Average speeds drop to 40 to 50 km/h once you include corners, villages and photo stops.
Mixed country roads (A-roads and B-roads): 300 to 450 km (185 to 280 miles), at average speeds of around 55 to 65 km/h.
Main roads and dual carriageways: 400 to 550 km (250 to 340 miles), averaging 70 to 80 km/h with fuel and food stops.
Motorways on a touring bike: 600 to 800 km (370 to 500 miles), averaging 90 to 100 km/h. Doable, but tiring, and not much fun to repeat day after day.
Small bikes and 125s: roughly two thirds of the figures above, because of lower cruising speeds, smaller tanks and more wind and vibration.

body.h: What really limits your daily distance

body.p: Fatigue is the biggest factor. Riding a motorcycle demands constant concentration, and the effects of tiredness creep up long before you feel sleepy: slower reactions, sloppier lines through corners and more missed hazards. Wind noise, vibration, heat and cold all add to it. Many experienced riders say that their riding quality drops noticeably after six to seven hours in the saddle, even with regular breaks.

Your bike matters too. Seat comfort, riding position and wind protection make a huge difference over a long day. A sports bike with a low bar and high pegs can become uncomfortable within two hours, while a touring bike with a big screen and upright position is built for all-day riding. Fuel range also sets your rhythm. A bike that does 200 km on a tank will force more stops than one that does 350 km, which is no bad thing for fatigue, but it does add time. If you are not sure of your bike's real range, the [fuel consumption calculator](/fuel-consumption-calculator) will work it out from a couple of fill-ups, and our guide on [how to work out motorcycle fuel consumption](/blog/how-to-work-out-motorcycle-fuel-consumption) explains the method.

The roads, the weather and daylight complete the picture. Rain slows you down and tires you faster, strong crosswinds are exhausting on motorways, and in autumn or winter you may only have eight or nine hours of usable daylight. Riding in the dark on unfamiliar roads is when a lot of touring mistakes happen, so plan to arrive with daylight to spare.

body.h: A worked example: planning a three-day trip

body.p: Say you want to ride a 1,200 km loop over three days on a mid-sized adventure bike, with a mix of main roads and country lanes. Here is how to turn that into realistic days.

ul: Split the distance: 1,200 km over three days is 400 km a day, which sits in the comfortable range for mixed roads.
Estimate average speed: on mixed roads, assume around 60 km/h including short stops. 400 km at 60 km/h is about 6 hours 40 minutes of riding.
Add proper breaks: a 15-minute stop every 90 minutes adds around 45 minutes, plus an hour for lunch. That brings the day to roughly 8.5 hours.
Check daylight: leaving at 8:30 means arriving around 17:00, which works in summer but is tight in late autumn.
Adjust the plan: if one day includes a mountain pass section, shorten it to 300 km and make another day a longer, faster main-road stretch.

body.p: The result is a plan you can actually stick to, rather than a single daily figure that looks fine on a map but leaves you riding at dusk on day two. Our guide on [how to plan a motorcycle trip](/blog/how-to-plan-a-motorcycle-trip) covers choosing routes and overnight stops in more detail.

body.h: Don't forget the bike's service schedule

body.p: A long trip can add a surprising amount of distance in one go. Three or four days at 400 km a day is 1,200 to 1,600 km, and a two-week tour can easily cover 4,000 km. If your bike has a 6,000 km oil change interval and you last changed the oil at 32,000 km, it is due at 38,000 km. Leave home at 35,500 km with a 4,000 km tour planned and you will pass that service halfway through the trip.

The [service due calculator](/service-due-calculator) makes that check quick, and it is worth doing before any multi-day ride. If a service will fall due on the road, either get it done early or plan where you will do it. Our checklist to [get your motorcycle ready for a long trip](/blog/get-your-motorcycle-ready-for-a-long-trip) covers tyres, chain, brakes and the rest of the pre-trip preparation.

body.h: How to ride further without wearing yourself out

body.p: If you want to build up to longer days, it is mostly about comfort and rhythm rather than toughness.

ul: Stop before you need to: a short break every 60 to 90 minutes keeps you fresher than pushing on until you are stiff and tired.
Drink water at every stop: mild dehydration hurts concentration, and it happens quickly in hot weather or behind a big screen.
Eat light: a heavy lunch makes the early afternoon the most tiring part of the day.
Wear earplugs: wind noise is a major cause of fatigue on long rides, especially above 90 km/h.
Dress for the conditions: being too cold or too hot drains energy faster than almost anything else.
Ride the faster stretches early: you are freshest in the morning, so get the motorway miles done first and save the scenic roads for when you can take them slower.
Build up gradually: if your longest day so far is 250 km, aim for 350 km before attempting 600 km.

body.h: Common mistakes when planning daily distances

body.p: The most common mistake is trusting the time a mapping app gives you. Those estimates assume car speeds and no stops, so a route listed at five hours often takes seven or more on a motorcycle once you add fuel, food, photos and rest breaks.

The second is planning every day at the top of your range. One long day is fine, but three in a row with no slack means one problem, such as a puncture or a road closure, cascades into riding late every evening. Build in at least one shorter day on a longer trip, and if you are riding with others, plan around the least experienced rider. Our guide on [how to ride in a group on a motorcycle trip](/blog/how-to-ride-in-a-group-on-a-motorcycle-trip) covers pacing a group in more detail.

ul: Type of roads: twisty, mixed, main roads or motorway?
Realistic average speed including short stops
Breaks every 60 to 90 minutes plus a proper lunch
Fuel stops based on your bike's real range
Arrival time with at least an hour of daylight to spare
Weather forecast, especially rain, heat and wind
Service due dates against the total trip distance
Spare time for wrong turns, closures and good views

body.p: For more ideas on planning routes and stops, browse our [motorcycle trips guides](/blog/trips). Once you have been on a few trips, your own records become the best guide of all: logging each day's distance in a [motorcycle mileage log](/motorcycle-mileage-log) shows you what you actually enjoy covering, rather than what looks possible on a map.

MotoLog lets you log trips and mileage and reminds you when services are due soon or overdue, so a long ride never sneaks past an oil change. If that sounds useful for your next trip, you can get the app below.

title: What counts as high mileage for a motorcycle?
alt: Black and white close-up of a worn motorcycle speedometer with a mechanical odometer showing over 72,000
excerpt: A big number on the odometer is not always a bad sign. Here is what counts as high mileage for different types of motorcycle, and why how the miles were covered matters more than how many there are.

body.p: Whether you are buying a used bike or wondering how much life is left in your own, the odometer is usually the first thing you look at. But there is no single number where a motorcycle suddenly becomes worn out. What counts as high mileage depends heavily on the type of bike, and even more on how it has been looked after.
As a rough guide, here is when many riders start to think of a bike as having covered a lot of distance:

ul: Small commuters and 125s: around 30,000 to 50,000 km, though many well-kept examples go much further
Sport bikes: around 40,000 to 60,000 km, since high-revving engines and hard riding take a toll
Middleweight naked and all-rounder bikes: around 60,000 to 80,000 km
Large touring bikes and big twins: often 100,000 km or more, as they are built to cover long distances at relaxed engine speeds

body.p: These are only rules of thumb. A carefully maintained bike can be in better health at 80,000 km than a neglected one at 20,000 km.

body.h: How the miles were covered matters

body.p: Long, steady motorway journeys are fairly gentle on an engine once it is warm. Short trips in town, where the engine rarely reaches full temperature, cause more wear per kilometre. Track days, heavy loads and hard launches add stress too. A bike that has done a lot of long-distance touring can actually be in better shape than one that has done a third of the distance in short hops.

body.h: Low mileage is not always good news

body.p: A bike that has barely moved for years can have problems of its own. Seals dry out, fuel goes stale, tyres harden with age and batteries die. If a low-mileage bike has spent long periods standing, check whether it was stored properly, as described in our guide to [storing a motorcycle for winter](/blog/how-to-store-your-motorcycle-for-winter).

The most useful thing to know about any bike's mileage is what was done at each stage. Regular oil changes, valve clearance checks, new chains and fresh fluids all add up to an engine that will keep going. When buying, ask for receipts and compare them with the mileage, and use a [used motorcycle checklist](/blog/buying-a-used-motorcycle-checklist) to spot signs of neglect. A full record also helps when you come to sell, as we explain in [why service history matters for resale value](/blog/service-history-motorcycle-resale-value).

Recording your mileage regularly gives you more than a number. It shows how far you ride each year, helps you spot an odometer that seems wrong, and lets you plan services before they are overdue rather than after.

title: Motorcycle fluids explained: what each one does and when to check it
seoTitle: Motorcycle fluids explained: what to check and when
alt: Close-up of a sport motorcycle's top yoke and handlebars, with the front brake and clutch fluid reservoirs showing amber fluid
excerpt: Oil, coolant, brake fluid, clutch fluid and fork oil all keep your motorcycle running safely. Here is what each fluid does, how to check it and roughly how often it needs changing.

body.p: A motorcycle relies on several different fluids, and each one has its own job. Some you can check in seconds before a ride, while others are changed only every couple of years. Knowing what they all do makes it much easier to keep on top of them, and to spot trouble before it turns into an expensive repair.

Oil lubricates and cools the engine, and on most bikes it also lubricates the gearbox and clutch. Check the level regularly, with the bike upright on level ground, using the sight glass or dipstick as your manual describes. Top up with the grade the manufacturer specifies. How often to change it depends on the bike and how you ride, which we cover in detail in [how often to change motorcycle oil](/blog/how-often-change-motorcycle-oil).

Liquid-cooled bikes use coolant to carry heat away from the engine and stop it freezing in winter. Check the level in the expansion tank when the engine is cold; it should sit between the minimum and maximum marks. Never open the radiator cap on a hot engine. Coolant breaks down over time, so most manufacturers recommend replacing it every two to three years.

Brake fluid transfers the force from your lever and pedal to the brake calipers. It absorbs moisture from the air, which lowers its boiling point and can make the brakes feel spongy after hard use. Check the level in each reservoir window, and look at the colour: fresh fluid is clear or light amber, while old fluid turns dark. Most bikes need new brake fluid about every two years. Our guide to [brake pads and fluid](/blog/motorcycle-brake-pads-and-fluid-when-to-replace) explains the signs to watch for.

Bikes with a hydraulic clutch use the same kind of fluid as the brakes, usually in a small reservoir on the left handlebar. It needs the same checks and is usually changed at the same time as the brake fluid. Bikes with a cable clutch do not have this fluid at all.

The front forks contain oil that controls how the suspension moves. It wears out slowly and is easy to forget, but tired fork oil can make the front end feel vague or bouncy. Change intervals vary a lot between models, so check your owner's manual. Oily residue on the fork legs can mean a leaking seal, which needs fixing soon.

ul: Check oil, coolant and brake fluid levels as part of your [quick pre-ride check](/blog/five-minute-pre-ride-check)
Look under the bike where you park it for fresh drips or stains
Use only the fluid types listed in your manual, and never mix brake fluid types
Write down the date and mileage whenever a fluid is changed

body.p: Because the longer intervals are easy to lose track of, a record really helps. MotoLog logs your mileage and services and reminds you when each one is due soon or overdue, so you can get the app just below and stop relying on memory.

title: What to do if your motorcycle breaks down on a trip
alt: A loaded touring motorcycle with luggage and a helmet stopped on a gravel verge beside a quiet country road
excerpt: A breakdown far from home is stressful, but a calm plan makes it much easier to handle. Here is what to do if your motorcycle stops on a trip, from getting safe to simple roadside checks and calling for help.

body.p: Most motorcycle trips go without a hitch, but sooner or later many riders find themselves at the side of the road with a bike that will not go. Being far from home makes it feel worse than it is. With a clear plan and a bit of preparation, a breakdown usually becomes a delay and a story rather than a disaster.

As soon as you feel something wrong, indicate and pull over somewhere safe, well away from moving traffic. On a fast road, get the bike as far onto the verge or hard shoulder as you can and stand behind a barrier if there is one. Switch on the hazard lights if your bike has them and keep your helmet and jacket on until you are clear of the road. If you are riding with others, the sweep rider should stop with you.

body.h: Simple checks before you call for help

body.p: Many roadside stops come down to something small. Once you are safe, go through the basics:

ul: Fuel: is there actually fuel in the tank, and is the fuel tap on if your bike has one?
Kill switch and side stand: both can stop the engine starting or cut it out
Battery and connections: a loose terminal is a common cause of sudden electrical failure, as our guide to [battery care](/blog/motorcycle-battery-care) explains
Fuses: a blown fuse can kill lights, ignition or the fuel pump, so carry spares
Tyres: check for punctures, nails or a slow leak
Chain: has it come off, snapped or become badly slack?

body.p: A small kit makes these checks possible, so pack the essentials from our [basic motorcycle toolkit](/blog/basic-motorcycle-toolkit-every-rider-should-own), along with a puncture repair kit and a compact pump or CO2 inflators.

If a warning light for oil pressure or temperature came on before the bike stopped, do not keep restarting it. Running an engine with no oil pressure can destroy it in minutes. The same goes for anything involving brakes, steering or a wheel. If the fix is not quick and obvious, it is time to call for help.

Before any long trip, check whether your insurance includes breakdown cover, and whether it works in every country you plan to ride through. Save the number in your phone and on a card in your wallet. When you call, have your exact location ready, ideally from your phone's map, along with your registration number and a short description of what happened.

Most breakdowns give some warning, and a bike that is fully serviced before a long ride is far less likely to let you down. Our checklist to [get your motorcycle ready for a long trip](/blog/get-your-motorcycle-ready-for-a-long-trip) covers what to look at in the days before you leave.

title: How to read a motorcycle tyre sidewall
alt: Low-angle close-up of a motorcycle front wheel showing the lettering on the tyre sidewall, parked on a road by large rocks
excerpt: The numbers and letters on your motorcycle tyre tell you its size, speed rating, load rating and age. Here is how to decode them so you buy the right replacement and spot tyres that are past their best.

body.p: Every motorcycle tyre carries a block of codes on its sidewall. At first glance it looks like a jumble of numbers and letters, but once you know the pattern you can read it in seconds. It tells you exactly which tyre fits your bike, how much weight and speed it is rated for, and how old it is.
A typical rear tyre might read 180/55 ZR17. Here is what each part means:

ul: 180 is the tyre's width in millimetres
55 is the aspect ratio: the height of the sidewall as a percentage of the width, so here it is 55 percent of 180 mm
Z is an older speed marking for tyres rated above 240 km/h, and R means radial construction
17 is the wheel rim diameter in inches

body.p: Older or smaller bikes may use bias-ply tyres, shown with a dash or a B instead of the R, or an older style of size such as 3.00-18. Always fit the sizes listed in your owner's manual or on the bike's tyre label.

After the size you will usually see something like 73W. The number is the load index, which tells you the maximum weight the tyre can carry at the correct pressure. The letter is the speed rating. Common ratings on road bikes include H (up to 210 km/h), V (up to 240 km/h) and W (up to 270 km/h). Never fit a tyre with a lower load index or speed rating than the manufacturer specifies.

ul: TL means tubeless and TT means the tyre needs an inner tube
M/C confirms the tyre is made for motorcycles
An arrow shows the direction of rotation, so the tyre must be fitted the right way round
Front and Rear markings show where a tyre is designed to go
Small triangles or TWI marks show where the tread wear indicators sit in the grooves

body.h: Check the age with the DOT code

body.p: Look for a code starting with DOT, ending in a four-digit number inside an oval. Those four digits are the week and year of manufacture, so 2324 means week 23 of 2024. Rubber hardens with age even when the tread looks fine, and many experts suggest replacing tyres around five years old regardless of wear. Our guide to [tyre pressure, tread and age](/blog/motorcycle-tyre-care-pressure-tread-and-age) covers this in more detail, and checking the date code is a smart step on any [used motorcycle you are thinking of buying](/blog/buying-a-used-motorcycle-checklist).

body.h: Keep a note when you change them

body.p: Tyres wear at different rates depending on how and where you ride. Writing down the date and odometer reading whenever you fit a new tyre shows you how many kilometres you really get from each set, which makes it much easier to plan replacements alongside your other [regular services](/blog/motorcycle-service-intervals-cheat-sheet).

title: How to choose a motorcycle jacket
alt: A rider in a black textile motorcycle jacket and helmet pulling on a glove beside his bike at the roadside
excerpt: A good motorcycle jacket protects you in a fall and keeps you comfortable in all weathers. Here is what to look for in materials, armour, fit and ventilation before you buy.

body.p: A riding jacket does more work than almost any other piece of kit. It protects your back, shoulders and elbows if you come off, keeps the wind and rain out, and decides whether a long ride is pleasant or miserable. With so many styles on the market, it helps to know what actually matters before you start trying them on.
Both can be excellent, and the right choice depends on how and when you ride:

ul: Leather offers the best abrasion resistance for its thickness and fits closely, which is why it is the favourite for sport riding. It is less practical in heavy rain and can be hot in summer.
Textile jackets are usually lighter, often waterproof, and come with removable thermal liners and vents. They suit commuting, touring and riding all year round.
Mesh jackets flow a lot of air for hot climates, but offer less abrasion protection, so look for good armour and reinforced panels.

body.p: In Europe, motorcycle clothing is tested to the EN 17092 standard. Ratings run from C (armour carrier only) through A, AA and AAA, with AAA offering the highest protection. For most road riding, an A or AA jacket is a sensible minimum. The label inside the jacket tells you the class.

Most jackets come with shoulder and elbow armour, but a back protector is often sold separately or is just a thin foam pad. Look for armour rated to EN 1621, with Level 2 offering more impact protection than Level 1. Upgrading to a proper Level 2 back protector is one of the cheapest safety improvements you can make.

Try jackets on in a riding position, leaning forward with your arms out as if holding the bars. The sleeves should still reach your wrists and overlap your gloves, and the armour should sit over your elbows and shoulders without sliding around. The jacket should be snug but not tight over a fleece in winter. If you ride with gauntlets, check the cuffs work with your [gloves](/blog/how-to-choose-motorcycle-gloves) rather than fighting them.

ul: Zip-out thermal liners let one jacket cover cold mornings and warm afternoons
Waterproof membranes keep you dry, but a separate waterproof oversuit can work better in heavy rain, as covered in our guide to [riding in the rain](/blog/how-to-ride-a-motorcycle-in-the-rain)
Vents on the chest, arms and back make a big difference in summer
Reflective panels and bright colours help you get seen in poor light
A connecting zip lets you join the jacket to matching trousers so it cannot ride up in a slide

body.p: A jacket works best as part of a full set, with proper trousers, gloves and [motorcycle boots](/blog/how-to-choose-motorcycle-boots). Clean it according to the label, reproof textiles now and then, and replace armour or the whole jacket after a serious crash.

title: How to ride in a group on a motorcycle trip
alt: A group of touring motorcycles riding in staggered formation along a dual carriageway past green trees under a blue sky
excerpt: Riding with friends is one of the best parts of motorcycling, but a group needs a little organisation to stay safe and together. Here is how to plan and ride a group trip that everyone enjoys.

body.p: A ride with friends can turn an ordinary route into a great day out. It can also turn into a stressful one if nobody knows where to stop, the group gets split at the first set of lights, or the fastest rider sets a pace the others cannot keep. A few simple habits make group riding safer and far more relaxed.

body.h: Agree the plan before you set off

body.p: Hold a quick briefing in the car park before anyone starts an engine. Cover the route, the planned stops for fuel and food, and what to do if someone gets lost. Share the route in advance so everyone has it on their phone or sat nav. If you are organising the day, our guide on [how to plan a motorcycle trip](/blog/how-to-plan-a-motorcycle-trip) helps you choose roads and stops that suit the whole group.

The bike with the smallest tank and the thirstiest engine decides how often you stop. Ask everyone roughly how far they get on a tank and plan fuel stops around the shortest range, with a margin. If you are not sure of your own figure, it is worth learning to [work out your fuel consumption](/blog/how-to-work-out-motorcycle-fuel-consumption) before the trip. Everyone should fill up at every stop, even if they think they can make the next one.

body.h: Choose a leader and a sweep

ul: The leader knows the route, sets a steady pace and signals hazards and turns early
The sweep rides at the back, ideally an experienced rider, and stops if anyone drops out or breaks down
Put newer or slower riders near the front, behind the leader, so the group's pace suits them
Keep groups to around six bikes; split larger groups into smaller ones that leave a few minutes apart

body.p: On straight roads, ride staggered: the leader on one side of the lane, the next rider on the other side about a second behind, and so on. This keeps the group compact while giving everyone space and a clear view ahead. In bends, at junctions and on poor surfaces, switch to single file and leave a proper gap. Never ride side by side in the same part of the lane.

The drop-off system stops the group splitting up at turns. At each junction, the rider behind the leader stops at a safe spot to mark the turn and waits until the sweep arrives. They then rejoin just ahead of the sweep. Nobody needs to rush through lights or take risks to keep up, because the turn is always marked.

A breakdown holds everyone up. Ask each rider to do a [quick pre-ride check](/blog/five-minute-pre-ride-check) on the morning of the trip, and make sure bikes are not overdue a service before a long day. A shared basic toolkit and a puncture repair kit in the sweep's luggage can save the day.

title: How to sell your motorcycle: prepare it, price it and close the deal
seoTitle: How to sell your motorcycle for the best price
alt: A clean yellow and black motorcycle parked by the kerb on a quiet sunny street in front of a brick house
excerpt: A little preparation can add real money to your sale price and make the whole process faster. Here is how to get your motorcycle ready to sell, set a fair price and hand it over safely.

body.p: Selling a motorcycle privately usually gets you a better price than trading it in, but only if you put in some work first. Buyers judge a bike in the first few minutes, and a tidy machine with a clear history sells faster and for more than a neglected one with the same mileage. Here is how to give yours the best chance.
You do not need to restore the bike, but fixing obvious niggles costs little and removes reasons for buyers to haggle:

ul: Clean and lube the chain and check its adjustment, following our guide to [chain maintenance](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance)
Check tyre pressures and tread depth, since worn tyres are an easy reason to knock money off
Make sure every light, indicator and the horn works
Replace cracked mirrors, missing bolts and tatty grips
Top up fluids and make sure the battery is charged so it starts first time

body.p: If a service is due soon, it is often worth doing it before you list the bike. A fresh service stamp is a strong selling point.

Put together the registration documents, spare keys, owner's manual and every receipt you can find. A complete record of services and repairs is one of the best ways to justify your asking price, as we explain in [why service history matters for resale value](/blog/service-history-motorcycle-resale-value). Buyers trust a bike more when they can see what has been done and when.

body.h: Clean it properly and take good photos

body.p: Wash the bike thoroughly, including the wheels and engine, and photograph it in daylight against a plain background. Take shots from both sides, the front and back, the dashboard showing the mileage, the tyres and any marks or damage. Being upfront about flaws builds trust and saves wasted viewings.

Look at listings for the same model, year and similar mileage, and note what they actually sell for rather than what people ask. Bikes with low mileage, a full history and recent work on tyres or chain can sit at the top of the range. Leave a little room for negotiation, since most buyers expect to talk the price down a bit.

Arrange viewings at your home or a public place during the day, and do not hand over keys for a test ride until you are happy. Many sellers ask for the full price in cash or a cleared payment before any test ride, or ask the buyer to hold a licence and insurance. Expect buyers to go through a checklist like our [used motorcycle buying checklist](/blog/buying-a-used-motorcycle-checklist), so go through it yourself first and you will not be caught off guard.

Only release the bike once payment has fully cleared. Write a simple receipt with both names, the date, the price, the mileage and the frame number, and keep a copy. Then notify the registration authority and cancel or transfer your insurance.

title: How to choose motorcycle boots
alt: A rider's tall black leather boot resting on the footboard of a large touring motorcycle, with chrome engine and wheel close up
excerpt: Your feet and ankles take a beating in even a minor fall. Here is what to look for in motorcycle boots, from protection and fit to waterproofing, so you buy a pair you will actually wear.

body.p: Boots are the piece of riding gear people most often skip. Plenty of riders who would never go out without a helmet will happily ride in trainers. The problem is that feet and ankles are among the most commonly injured parts of the body in motorcycle crashes, and even a simple drop at a junction can trap a foot under the bike. A good pair of boots is cheap insurance.
Motorcycle boots are built to do things everyday shoes cannot:

ul: Resist abrasion if you slide along the road
Stop the ankle from twisting or crushing under the weight of the bike
Protect the shin and ankle bones from impacts
Keep the sole stiff so your foot is not bent the wrong way
Stay on your feet in a crash, which laces alone often do not

body.p: Look for boots tested to the European standard EN 13634. The label shows ratings for height, abrasion resistance, impact cut resistance and transverse rigidity, with 2 being the higher level for each.
The best boot depends on how you ride:

ul: Touring boots are tall, usually waterproof and comfortable to walk in, which suits long days and trips
Sport boots are stiffer, with sliders and strong ankle bracing for fast road and track riding
Adventure boots combine tall protection with a grippy sole for gravel and off-road stops
Short urban boots and riding trainers look like normal shoes and are better than nothing, but offer less ankle and shin protection

body.p: Try boots on in the afternoon, when feet are slightly larger, and wear the socks you ride in. Your heel should not lift when you walk, and your toes should not touch the end. Then sit on a bike if you can. Check you can feel and work the gear lever easily, since a bulky toe box can make gear changes clumsy. As with [choosing gloves](/blog/how-to-choose-motorcycle-gloves), comfort matters: boots you dislike wearing tend to stay in the cupboard.

If you ride all year, a waterproof membrane is worth paying for. Wet feet get cold fast, and cold riders lose concentration. Our tips for [riding in the rain](/blog/how-to-ride-a-motorcycle-in-the-rain) cover the rest of a wet weather setup. In hot climates, a vented boot may suit you better, as long as it still has proper ankle protection.

Clean off road grime and salt after wet rides, let boots dry naturally away from direct heat, and treat leather now and then so it does not crack. Check soles, zips and buckles as part of your [pre-ride check](/blog/five-minute-pre-ride-check), and replace boots that have been through a crash, just as you would a [helmet after an impact](/blog/how-to-choose-a-motorcycle-helmet).

title: How to work out your motorcycle's fuel consumption
alt: A rider in a full-face helmet sitting on a motorcycle at a petrol station forecourt in warm evening light, with scooters at the pumps behind
excerpt: Knowing how far your bike goes on a tank helps you plan rides and spot problems early. Here is a simple way to measure your motorcycle's real fuel consumption and what to do if it gets worse.

body.p: Most riders have a rough idea of how far they get on a tank, but very few know the real number. That is a shame, because fuel consumption is one of the best early warnings you have. A bike that suddenly needs more fuel to cover the same distance is often telling you something needs attention, long before a warning light comes on.
The most reliable way to measure consumption needs nothing more than your odometer and a fuel receipt:

ul: Fill the tank to the same level every time, ideally at the same pump, and note the odometer reading
Ride normally until you next need fuel
Fill to the same level again and note how many litres it took and the new odometer reading
Divide the litres by the distance and multiply by 100 to get litres per 100 km

body.p: For example, if you rode 280 km and it took 14 litres to fill up again, that is 14 ÷ 280 × 100 = 5 litres per 100 km. If you prefer kilometres per litre, divide the distance by the litres instead: 280 ÷ 14 = 20 km per litre. Do this over three or four tanks and take the average, since a single fill can be thrown off by a short trip or a pump that clicks off early.

body.h: Why the dashboard figure is not enough

body.p: Many modern bikes show an average consumption figure, and it is useful for a quick check. But it is an estimate, and it can be optimistic by several percent. Working it out from real fill-ups gives you an honest baseline you can compare against over months and seasons. That is one more reason it pays to [track your mileage](/blog/why-track-motorcycle-mileage) properly rather than relying on memory.
Some changes are normal. Cold weather, heavy luggage, a passenger, motorway speeds and stop-start traffic will all push the figure up. If none of those explain it, look at the bike itself:

ul: Low tyre pressures add rolling resistance, so check them as part of your [tyre care routine](/blog/motorcycle-tyre-care-pressure-tread-and-age)
A dirty air filter makes the engine work harder, which our guide to [cleaning or replacing the air filter](/blog/motorcycle-air-filter-when-to-clean-or-replace) covers
A dry or tight chain wastes power between the engine and the rear wheel
Worn spark plugs or an overdue service can leave the engine running less efficiently
Dragging brakes, which you can often feel as warmth in the disc after a ride

body.h: Use it to plan your range

body.p: Once you know your real consumption and your tank size, you know your real range. Take that number, knock off a safety margin of around 20 percent, and you have a figure you can trust when [planning a longer trip](/blog/how-to-plan-a-motorcycle-trip) through areas where fuel stations are far apart.

title: Motorcycle air filter: when to clean or replace it
alt: A mechanic sitting on a stool beside a scooter engine and rear wheel stripped down on a workshop floor, with tools laid out in front
excerpt: A clogged air filter quietly costs you power and fuel. Here is how often to check your motorcycle's air filter, how to tell when it needs attention, and whether to clean or replace it.

body.p: The air filter is one of the easiest parts of a motorcycle to forget. It sits out of sight under the seat, tank or a side panel, and it rarely fails in a dramatic way. Instead, it slowly fills with dust, bugs and grime until the engine has to work harder for every breath. Looking after it is cheap, quick and one of the best things you can do for how your bike runs.

Your engine burns a mix of fuel and air, and it needs a lot of air. The filter stops dust and grit from being drawn into the engine, where it would wear the cylinders, piston rings and valves. A clean filter lets air through freely while catching the dirt. A blocked one restricts airflow, which can make the engine run rich, feel flat and use more fuel.

Most manufacturers list an air filter check or replacement every 10,000 to 20,000 km, or at set services. Your owner's manual has the exact figure, and our [service intervals cheat sheet](/blog/motorcycle-service-intervals-cheat-sheet) shows where it usually fits alongside oil, plugs and valves. Check more often if you:

ul: Ride on gravel, dirt or dusty roads
Spend a lot of time in heavy city traffic
Ride in areas with lots of pollen, sand or insects
Have just come back from a long trip on mixed roads

body.p: A dirty filter does not always announce itself, but there are clues. The bike may feel sluggish when you open the throttle, fuel economy may drop, or the engine may hesitate or run unevenly. Once you can get to the filter, look at it against the light. If it is dark, caked with dirt or you can barely see light through it, it is time to act.
It depends on the type of filter your bike uses:

ul: Paper filters are the most common on road bikes. They cannot be washed, so replace them when they are dirty. You can gently tap out loose dust between changes, but never blow compressed air through from the clean side or soak them.
Foam filters, common on off-road bikes, are washed in filter cleaner or warm soapy water, dried fully and re-oiled with proper foam filter oil.
Oiled cotton gauze filters are cleaned with a dedicated kit and lightly re-oiled. Too much oil can foul sensors, so follow the kit's instructions.

body.p: Whatever the type, make sure the filter seats properly and the airbox lid seals all the way round. A filter that lets air bypass it is worse than a dirty one. A few basic tools from a [rider's toolkit](/blog/basic-motorcycle-toolkit-every-rider-should-own) are usually all you need to get to it.

Because the air filter is checked so rarely, it is easy to lose track of when it was last done. Write down the date and the odometer reading each time you clean or replace it. A record like this also adds weight to your [service history when you sell](/blog/service-history-motorcycle-resale-value), since buyers like to see the small jobs were done too.

title: Motorcycle warning lights explained: what each one means
alt: A lit digital motorcycle instrument cluster at night showing neutral, the odometer and an amber oil warning light
excerpt: A light on the dash can mean anything from a reminder to a reason to stop right now. Here is what the common motorcycle warning lights mean and what to do about each one.

body.p: Modern motorcycles have more warning lights than ever, and it is not always obvious which ones matter. Some are simply information, some mean you should get the bike checked soon, and a few mean you should pull over as soon as it is safe. The exact symbols vary between manufacturers, so your owner's manual is the final word, but most bikes follow the same broad rules.
Colour is the quickest guide to how serious a light is:

ul: Green or blue lights are information, such as neutral, indicators or high beam
Amber or yellow lights mean something needs attention soon, but you can usually ride on carefully
Red lights mean stop as soon as it is safe and find out what is wrong

body.p: Usually red and shaped like an oil can. If it comes on while riding, stop as soon as you safely can and switch off the engine. Low oil pressure can destroy an engine in minutes. Check the oil level once the bike has stood for a few minutes, and do not ride on if the light stays on after topping up. Keeping to sensible [oil change intervals](/blog/how-often-change-motorcycle-oil) makes this far less likely.

Often red, with a thermometer symbol. It means the engine is running too hot. Stop, let it cool, and check the coolant level once the engine is cold. Never open a hot radiator cap. A temperature light in slow summer traffic can point to a cooling fan that is not switching on.

A red or amber battery symbol means the charging system is not keeping the battery topped up. The bike may run for a while on what is left in the battery, but it will eventually stop. Head home or to a garage by the shortest route, and turn off heated grips and other accessories to save power. Our guide to [motorcycle battery care](/blog/motorcycle-battery-care) explains how to test the battery afterwards.

The ABS light normally comes on when you switch on and goes out once you ride off. If it stays on, the anti-lock system may be switched off because of a fault, but the normal brakes still work. Ride gently, leave extra stopping room, and get it checked, along with a look at the [brake pads and fluid](/blog/motorcycle-brake-pads-and-fluid-when-to-replace).

Usually amber and shaped like an engine. It means the bike's computer has spotted a fault. If the bike runs normally you can usually ride on carefully and get it diagnosed soon. If it flashes, or the bike misfires or loses power, stop and get help.

Many bikes show a spanner symbol when a service is due based on time or mileage. It is not a fault, but it is easy to ignore until it becomes one. Our [service intervals cheat sheet](/blog/motorcycle-service-intervals-cheat-sheet) covers what each service usually includes.

title: How to pack a motorcycle for a weekend trip
alt: A black cruiser motorcycle with a brown leather saddlebag and a helmet on the seat, parked against a weathered concrete wall
excerpt: Packing a motorcycle is a balancing act, literally. Here is what to bring for a weekend away, how to carry it, and how to load the bike so it still handles well.

body.p: A weekend away is one of the best ways to enjoy a motorcycle, but you cannot just throw a suitcase in the boot. Space is tight, weight changes how the bike handles, and anything badly strapped down can work loose at speed. With a bit of planning, though, two or three days of kit fits easily on almost any bike.
The most common mistake is bringing too much. Lay out everything you plan to take, then put a third of it back. A weekend usually needs:

ul: One change of riding base layers and one set of casual clothes
Light shoes, so you are not walking around all evening in boots
A waterproof oversuit or rain layer, even if the forecast looks good
Toiletries in small travel bottles
Phone charger, a power bank and any cables for your intercom or sat nav
A small kit of tools, a puncture repair kit and a torch, ideally the [basic toolkit](/blog/basic-motorcycle-toolkit-every-rider-should-own) you already carry

body.p: Soft saddlebags, a tail bag and a tank bag cover most weekend trips and fit almost any bike. Hard panniers and top boxes are lockable and fully waterproof, but they need mounting racks. Whatever you use, line soft bags with dry bags or bin liners, because very few are truly waterproof in a long downpour. Keep the things you need during the day, like a rain layer, documents and snacks, in the tank bag or the top of a tail bag where you can reach them quickly.

body.h: Load the bike for good handling

body.p: Where the weight goes matters as much as how much there is. Heavy items should sit low and as close to the middle of the bike as possible, so put dense things like tools and shoes at the bottom of the saddlebags and keep the tail bag and top box for light, bulky clothing. Balance the weight evenly between left and right.

Check every strap after the first few miles, because loads settle once you start riding. Make sure nothing can touch the exhaust, the rear tyre or the chain, and that no loose strap ends can flap into the wheel.

body.h: Adjust the bike, not just the bags

body.p: Extra weight, especially with a passenger, changes how the bike behaves. Most owner's manuals list a higher tyre pressure for a loaded bike, and many bikes let you add rear preload to stop the back end sagging. Brakes will need a little more distance too, so leave bigger gaps on the road. Before you set off, run through your usual [pre-ride check](/blog/five-minute-pre-ride-check) with the bike fully loaded.

body.h: Plan around the bike as well as the route

body.p: A weekend trip can add a few hundred miles in two days, so it is worth knowing whether a service or chain adjustment is due before you leave. Our guides to [planning a trip you will enjoy](/blog/how-to-plan-a-motorcycle-trip) and [getting your bike ready for a long trip](/blog/get-your-motorcycle-ready-for-a-long-trip) cover the rest.

title: Motorcycle battery care: how to keep it charged and healthy
alt: A black bobber motorcycle parked in a dim underground garage under fluorescent lights
excerpt: A flat battery is one of the most common reasons a motorcycle will not start. Here is why bike batteries die, how to test yours, and how to make it last.

body.p: Few things spoil a planned ride faster than pressing the starter and hearing a weak click. Motorcycle batteries are small, they often sit unused for weeks, and many modern bikes draw a little power even when they are switched off. The good news is that most battery problems are avoidable with a few simple habits.

A car battery gets a long charge every time you drive, but a motorcycle often does short trips or sits in the garage between weekends. Alarms, immobilisers, clocks and ECUs all draw a small current around the clock, and over two or three weeks that is enough to drain a small battery. Cold weather makes things worse, because a cold battery delivers less power just when the engine needs more to turn over.
Batteries also wear out with age. Most last somewhere between three and five years, and every time one is run completely flat it loses some of its capacity for good.

body.h: Check it before it lets you down

body.p: A cheap digital multimeter tells you most of what you need to know. With the bike off and rested for a few hours, measure across the terminals:

ul: Around 12.6 to 12.8 volts means the battery is fully charged
Around 12.4 volts means it is about three-quarters charged and worth topping up
Below about 12.2 volts means it is low and should be charged soon
If it will not hold a charge for a day or two after charging, it is probably time for a new one

body.p: While you are there, look at the terminals. White or green crust on the connections can stop current flowing properly. Clean it off with a wire brush, tighten the bolts and add a thin smear of terminal grease. You can fold this into your [pre-ride check](/blog/five-minute-pre-ride-check) every few weeks.

The single best thing you can do for a motorcycle battery is connect it to a smart charger, sometimes called a battery tender or maintainer, whenever the bike will sit for more than a week or two. A smart charger brings the battery up to full and then holds it there without overcharging. Many come with a lead that you can leave permanently attached to the battery, so plugging in takes seconds. It is essential if you are [storing your bike for winter](/blog/how-to-store-your-motorcycle-for-winter).
Make sure the charger suits your battery type. Lithium batteries, which are increasingly common on newer bikes, need a charger with a lithium mode, and using the wrong setting can damage them.

Short trips of a few minutes use more charge to start the engine than the charging system can put back. If most of your riding is short hops, try to fit in a longer ride of half an hour or more every week or so, or put the bike on the charger afterwards.

Because batteries fade gradually, it is easy to forget how old yours is until it fails on a cold morning. Note the date you fit a new one, and treat a check of the battery as part of your regular [maintenance schedule](/blog/motorcycle-maintenance-schedule), alongside jobs like [changing the oil](/blog/how-often-change-motorcycle-oil).

title: How to choose motorcycle gloves
alt: A pair of black leather motorcycle gloves resting on a chrome speedometer and handlebars
excerpt: Your hands work the throttle, brakes and clutch, and they are usually the first thing to touch the ground in a fall. Here is how to pick gloves that protect them and still let you ride well.

body.p: Gloves are easy to treat as an afterthought, but your hands do more on a motorcycle than any other part of your body. They control the throttle, the front brake and the clutch, and in a fall they are almost always the first thing to hit the road. A good pair protects you, keeps you comfortable and lets you operate the controls precisely. A bad pair does none of those things well.

Look for gloves certified to EN 13594, the European standard for motorcycle gloves. Level 1 is the basic pass and Level 2 means better abrasion and impact performance; the label inside the cuff will tell you which. Beyond the label, check for:

ul: Hard or foam armour over the knuckles
Reinforced palm sliders, the part that usually touches the ground first
A secure closure at the wrist so the glove cannot come off in a slide
Double or hidden stitching on the seams, which is less likely to burst

body.p: A glove should be snug without pinching. With your fingers stretched out, the tips should just touch the ends of the glove, and when you make a fist there should be no tight spots across the knuckles. Try them on while holding a handlebar if the shop has one, or at least curl your hand around something of the same size. Leather will relax a little with use, so a pair that is slightly firm at first usually ends up fitting well, while a pair that is loose on day one only gets looser.

Fit also affects control. Thick, baggy gloves make it harder to feel the brake lever and to make small throttle adjustments. Do a few slow laps of a car park in new gloves before a longer ride, the same way you would when [practising low-speed control](/blog/five-riding-skills-to-practise-in-a-car-park).
Most riders who ride all year end up with at least two pairs, because no single glove works well in every season.

ul: Summer gloves are short-cuffed and vented, often leather with mesh panels, so your hands do not get sweaty and lose grip.
Winter gloves have insulation and a long gauntlet that seals over your jacket sleeve. They are warmer but bulkier, so expect slightly less feel at the levers.

Waterproof gloves use a membrane to keep rain out. They are worth having if you ride in the wet often, and they pair well with the techniques in our guide to [riding in the rain](/blog/how-to-ride-a-motorcycle-in-the-rain).

body.p: If you only buy one pair, choose a mid-weight leather glove with a gauntlet and good armour. It will cover most of the riding most people do.

Leather gloves last longer and stay supple if you clean them gently and apply a leather conditioner now and then. Let wet gloves dry naturally rather than on a radiator, which can crack the leather and shrink the fit. Check the stitching and closures as part of your [pre-ride check](/blog/five-minute-pre-ride-check), and replace gloves after a crash even if they look fine, the same as you would a [helmet](/blog/how-to-choose-a-motorcycle-helmet).

title: Motorcycle tyre care: pressure, tread and age
alt: Front wheel and tyre of a red motorcycle in motion on smooth asphalt
excerpt: Two small contact patches are all that hold your motorcycle to the road. Here is how to check tyre pressure, tread and age, and when it is time for a new pair.

body.p: Everything a motorcycle does, from braking to cornering to riding through a wet roundabout, happens through two contact patches roughly the size of your palm. Tyres are also one of the easiest parts to neglect, because they wear slowly and still look round and black long after they have stopped performing well. A few minutes of checking every week or two keeps them doing their job.

Motorcycle tyres lose air gradually, even without a puncture, and a tyre that is a few psi low makes the steering feel heavy, wears the edges faster and runs hotter. Check pressures at least every couple of weeks and before any longer ride, always with the tyres cold, before you have ridden more than a mile or two. Use your own gauge rather than a forecourt one, and set the pressures listed in your owner's manual or on the sticker on the swingarm or chain guard. Many manuals give a higher figure for riding with a passenger or luggage, so adjust for that too.

Most tyres have small wear indicator bars moulded into the bottom of the grooves, marked by a small triangle or the letters TWI on the sidewall. When the tread is level with those bars, the tyre is finished. Many riders change well before that point, because grip in the wet drops off noticeably as the grooves get shallow. Check the legal minimum where you live as well, since it is often higher than people expect.

While you are looking, check how the tyre is wearing. A flat strip down the middle of the rear is normal for a bike that does a lot of straight-line miles, but it makes the bike reluctant to lean. Uneven or stepped wear can point to wrong pressures or a suspension problem worth looking into.
Run your eyes and hand around both tyres and look for:

ul: Nails, screws or stones lodged in the tread
Cuts, bulges or blisters on the tread or sidewall
Fine cracks in the rubber, especially on the sidewalls
A tyre that keeps losing pressure faster than the other one

body.p: Anything that looks like a bulge or a deep cut means the tyre should be replaced, not ridden home and forgotten about.

Rubber hardens with time, even on a bike that sits in the garage most of the year. An old tyre with plenty of tread can still have far less grip than a new one. The manufacturing date is printed on the sidewall as a four-digit code after the letters DOT: the first two digits are the week and the last two are the year, so 2223 means week 22 of 2023. Many manufacturers suggest an inspection by a tyre specialist once a tyre is five years old and replacement by around ten years at the latest, whatever the tread looks like.

body.h: Make it part of your routine

body.p: The easiest way to stay on top of tyres is to tie the checks to things you already do. Check pressures each time you fill up, look over the tread when you clean [the chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance), and note the mileage whenever you fit a new pair so you know roughly how long your tyres last on your bike and your roads.

title: How to ride a motorcycle in the rain
alt: Rider's view over the handlebars of a motorcycle on a wet, rain-soaked country road
excerpt: Rain does not have to end a ride. Smooth inputs, the right lines and a bike in good shape make wet roads far less stressful. Here is how to ride them with confidence.

body.p: Sooner or later every rider gets caught in the rain. Riding on wet roads is not dangerous in itself, but it leaves you much less margin for error. Grip is lower, braking distances are longer, and other drivers see you less easily. The good news is that a few habits make a big difference, and most of them are things you can practise on every ride.

In the dry, a tyre can forgive a rushed brake or a sudden handful of throttle. In the wet it often cannot. The aim is to ask the tyres for one thing at a time, gently. Roll the throttle on and off rather than snapping it, squeeze the brakes progressively instead of grabbing them, and finish most of your braking while the bike is upright, before you turn in. Steering should be calm and deliberate too, so set your speed early and keep the bike settled through the corner.

body.h: Leave more space and slow down earlier

body.p: Stopping distances on a wet road can easily double. Open the gap to the vehicle ahead to at least four seconds, and start slowing for junctions and bends sooner than you normally would. Extra space also gives you time to read the surface ahead, which matters more in the rain than almost anything else.

Some parts of the road lose far more grip than the tarmac around them when wet. Pick a line that keeps the tyres off them where you can, and stay upright and off the brakes when you have to cross one.

ul: Painted road markings, zebra crossings and arrows
Manhole covers, drain grates and metal plates
The oily strip in the centre of the lane, especially after the first rain in a while
Fallen leaves, mud and gravel washed out of field entrances
Standing water, which can hide potholes and cause aquaplaning

body.p: Rain and spray make you harder to spot, so wear something bright or reflective and ride with your lights on. Comfort is a safety issue as well. A rider who is cold and soaked loses concentration and gets tense on the bars, which is the opposite of the loose, smooth style the wet demands. Proper waterproofs, gloves that still grip when wet and an anti-fog visor or Pinlock insert are worth the money.

body.h: Your bike has to be ready too

body.p: Technique only works if the motorcycle holds up its end. Tyres are the most important part: worn tread clears much less water, and tyres that are underinflated or past their best lose grip early. Check pressures and tread depth regularly, not just when the forecast turns. Brakes need healthy pads and fresh fluid to stay progressive, and a [chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance) that has just been through a wet ride wants cleaning and lubing before it starts to rust.

A wet ride is also a good reason to note what the bike went through. Logging the trip and the [mileage](/blog/why-track-motorcycle-mileage) tells you when tyres, chain and brakes are really due for a look, rather than leaving you to guess.

The best time to learn how your bike feels in the wet is on a quiet road with no pressure, not in heavy traffic on the way home. Take a short ride on a damp day, keep everything smooth, and build up gradually. Confidence in the rain comes from experience, and every calm wet ride adds to it.

title: Motorcycle brakes: when to replace pads and fluid
alt: Close-up of a motorcycle's front brake disc and caliper behind the fork leg
excerpt: Brakes wear slowly, so the change is easy to miss until it matters. Here is how to check your pads and fluid, and how often to replace them.

body.p: Brakes are the one system on a motorcycle you cannot afford to get wrong, and they are also the one that tells you least about its condition. Pads wear a fraction of a millimetre at a time, and brake fluid ages without any change you would notice on a normal ride. By the time the lever feels different, you are already overdue.

Most calipers let you see the pads from the side or from below with a torch. Look at the friction material between the backing plate and the disc. Many pads have a wear groove cut into the material; once the groove is gone, the pads are finished. As a rough guide, if there is less than about 2 mm of material left, replace them. Your service manual gives the exact minimum for your bike.
Check both front calipers and the rear. Fronts usually wear faster, but a rear that is used heavily in town or with a passenger can surprise you.

ul: A squeal or grinding noise when you brake.
The lever or pedal travels further than it used to, or feels spongy.
The bike pulls or the brakes judder under firm braking.
Scoring or a visible lip on the edge of the disc.
Brake fluid in the reservoir looks dark rather than light amber.

body.h: Brake fluid ages even when you don't ride

body.p: Most motorcycle brake fluid absorbs moisture from the air over time. Water in the fluid lowers its boiling point, so after a long descent or hard braking the fluid can boil and the lever can go soft. That is why manufacturers specify a fluid change by time, commonly every two years, regardless of how far you ride. If you can't remember when the fluid was last changed, assume it is due.

body.h: Discs and the rest of the system

body.p: Discs wear too, more slowly than pads. The minimum thickness is usually stamped on the disc itself. While you are looking, check the brake lines for cracks or bulges and make sure nothing is leaking around the caliper or master cylinder. Anything that looks wrong here is worth a professional opinion before your next ride.

Because brakes wear on two clocks, distance for pads and time for fluid, they are easy to lose track of. Note when you change pads with the odometer reading, and note the date of each fluid change. That record makes the next check obvious instead of a guess.
